selection.method: highest remaining verified actor-primary profiles after Batch 18

profiles.name: Ted Johnstone
profiles.excerpt: Ted Johnstone was a versatile WXYZ repertory actor heard across The Lone Ranger and Challenge of the Yukon, where he even supplied the vocalizations of Yukon King.
profiles.bio_html:
Ted Johnstone belonged to the Detroit acting company that powered WXYZ's adventure programs. He worked as a supporting player on The Lone Ranger, moving among changing characters rather than being tied to one continuing human role.

Johnstone also contributed to Challenge of the Yukon. After sound-effects man Dewey Cole, the vocalizations of Yukon King were supplied by Johnstone, an unusual example of a radio actor using voice alone to portray an animal character within a realistic adventure series.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 29 The Lone Ranger performances credited to Johnstone. Those broadcasts document his place within the WXYZ repertory that supplied the series with a constantly changing cast of supporting characters.

profiles.name: Ellen Morgan
profiles.excerpt: Ellen Morgan was a dependable dramatic radio actress whose surviving work is especially strong in Suspense and Crime Classics.
profiles.bio_html:
Ellen Morgan belongs to the network-radio repertory whose professional record survives more clearly in broadcasts and cast lists than in later biographical accounts. Her credits place her repeatedly in sophisticated dramatic productions during the 1940s and 1950s.

Morgan appeared frequently on Suspense and also worked on Crime Classics, Lux Radio Theatre, CBS Radio Workshop and Escape. Those programs demanded actors capable of moving from contemporary crime to historical reconstruction and psychological drama without relying on a continuing character.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 18 Suspense performances credited to Morgan, five Crime Classics appearances, three Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts and additional work on CBS Radio Workshop and Escape.

profiles.name: Horace Braham
profiles.excerpt: Horace Braham brought a long Broadway career and a commanding British stage voice into American radio drama, including a substantial run on Whitehall 1212.
profiles.bio_html:
Horace Braham was born in London in 1892 and built a long theatrical career before and during his years in American radio. His Broadway work stretched across decades and included roles in Julius Caesar, Antigone and Witness for the Prosecution.

Radio used Braham's formal stage delivery in literary, mystery and crime programs. Whitehall 1212 became the strongest surviving concentration of his microphone work, while Columbia Workshop, Inner Sanctum Mysteries and wartime drama showed a wider repertory range.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 20 Whitehall 1212 performances credited to Braham, two Columbia Workshop appearances and additional work on Cloak and Dagger, Inner Sanctum Mysteries, Stroke of Fate, The Big Show, The Chase and Words at War.

profiles.name: Jack Carol
profiles.excerpt: Jack Carol was a working radio character actor whose surviving credits range from Sears Radio Theater and Rocky Fortune to western, detective and anthology drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Jack Carol is another professional radio actor whose broadcast record is more complete than the surviving personal biography. His credits span several decades and show the flexibility expected of repertory performers who moved constantly among formats.

Carol's strongest surviving GRH concentration is Sears Radio Theater, supplemented by appearances on Rocky Fortune, Barrie Craig, Escape, Father Knows Best, NBC University Theater, Night Beat and Screen Directors Playhouse.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 19 Sears Radio Theater performances credited to Carol, two Rocky Fortune appearances and single broadcasts across six additional dramatic series.

profiles.name: Kermit Murdock
profiles.excerpt: Kermit Murdock became a familiar radio voice in science fiction and experimental drama before film and television cast him as professors, judges and other men of authority.
profiles.bio_html:
Kermit Murdock was born in Pittsburgh in 1908 and built a career across radio, film and television. His controlled, thoughtful delivery made him particularly effective in roles that required intellectual authority or quiet menace.

Radio placed Murdock in X Minus One, Quiet, Please, The Chase and other dramatic anthologies. His later screen work included In the Heat of the Night, The Andromeda Strain and television roles that often used the same professorial presence familiar from his radio work.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves eight The Chase performances credited to Murdock, six X Minus One appearances, four Quiet, Please episodes, two each on Columbia Workshop, Stroke of Fate and Words at War, plus additional anthology work.

profiles.name: Lee Millar Jr.
profiles.excerpt: Lee Millar Jr. grew up inside a professional radio family and became a busy supporting actor across westerns, comedy, literary anthology and later television.
profiles.bio_html:
Lee Millar Jr. was the son of actress Verna Felton and actor Lee Millar, placing him inside a family deeply connected to radio and voice performance. He developed his own career as an actor rather than merely inheriting a famous surname.

Millar worked across westerns, comedy and anthology drama, appearing on programs including Gunsmoke, NBC University Theater, Sears Radio Theater, Broadway Is My Beat and Fibber McGee and Molly. That spread shows a supporting player valued for adaptability across very different tones.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves four performances each on Gunsmoke and NBC University Theater credited to Millar, three Sears Radio Theater appearances, two each on Broadway Is My Beat, Fibber McGee and Molly, Lux Radio Theatre, The Adventures of Philip Marlowe and The Halls of Ivy.

profiles.name: Warren William
profiles.excerpt: Warren William brought the urbane authority of his film career to radio, including the title role in Strange Wills and starring appearances on Lux Radio Theatre.
profiles.bio_html:
Warren William was born Warren William Krech in Minnesota in 1894 and became one of Warner Bros.' defining leading men of the early 1930s. His screen persona often combined charm, ambition and moral ambiguity, qualities that translated naturally to dramatic radio.

William's most substantial continuing radio work was Strange Wills, a psychological anthology built around unusual inheritances and the conflicts they created. He also starred in Lux Radio Theatre adaptations and appeared on Suspense, bringing a polished film-star voice into both anthology and mystery formats.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 26 Strange Wills performances credited to William and two Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts. That concentrated run makes Strange Wills the clear center of his GRH radio profile.

profiles.name: William Quinn
profiles.excerpt: William Quinn was a versatile New York radio actor whose surviving work is especially strong in Suspense, X Minus One and wartime anthology drama.
profiles.bio_html:
William Quinn belongs to the New York radio repertory whose professional identity is best reconstructed from the broadcasts themselves. His credits span wartime drama, science fiction, crime and anthology production across more than a decade.

Quinn appeared repeatedly on both Suspense and X Minus One, while Words at War, The Chase and Dimension X used him in changing supporting roles. The range of those programs reflects a performer comfortable with both realistic drama and speculative material.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves six performances each on Suspense and X Minus One credited to Quinn, four Words at War appearances, three The Chase episodes, two Dimension X broadcasts and additional work on several other series.

profiles.name: Cliff Clark
profiles.excerpt: Cliff Clark carried a long film-character career into radio as a dependable Lux Radio Theatre stock player, often recreating the authority figures he specialized in on screen.
profiles.bio_html:
Cliff Clark was born in New York City in 1889 and developed into one of Hollywood's busiest supporting actors. Film audiences repeatedly saw him as policemen, officials, judges and other authority figures, a screen type built around his direct delivery and sturdy presence.

Radio used Clark in much the same way. Lux Radio Theatre repeatedly cast him in supporting roles around major stars, including adaptations in which he sometimes recreated or reshaped parts connected to films he had appeared in. His value lay in making small roles sound immediately complete.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 27 Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Clark. That concentrated body of work documents his place inside the program's dependable Hollywood stock company.

profiles.name: Jada Rowland
profiles.excerpt: Jada Rowland moved from child performance and Broadway into daytime television and later became one of CBS Radio Mystery Theater's recurring dramatic actresses.
profiles.bio_html:
Jada Rowland was born on Staten Island in 1943 and began acting while still young. She worked on Broadway and television and became especially familiar to daytime audiences through long-running roles on The Secret Storm, As the World Turns and The Doctors.

Rowland later became a frequent performer on CBS Radio Mystery Theater, where the repertory format let her move far beyond one soap-opera identity. She eventually left acting and developed a second creative career as an illustrator of children's books, extending her visual creativity well beyond performance.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 27 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Rowland. Those broadcasts capture the radio-drama side of a career otherwise strongly associated with stage and daytime television.
